Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is usu-
ally evaluated from one observed trace: the
query, the retrieved context, and the generated
answer. Such evaluations can tell us whether
the answer is consistent with the retrieved con-
text, but not whether the system would still
give the same answer if that context were re-
moved, updated, or contradicted. We intro-
duce COUNTERMEM, an evaluation protocol
for RAG systems that are expected to answer
from retrieved evidence: it keeps the RAG
configuration fixed, changes only the retrieved
context, regenerates the answer, and records
whether the answer changes in the expected di-
rection. Across RAGBench, ExpertQA, and
DelucionQA, COUNTERMEM complements
observed-trace faithfulness by exposing fail-
ures it is not designed to see. Configurations
that look equivalent under RAGAS faithfulness
behave very differently once their evidence is
removed, updated, or contradicted, and among
RAGChecker-approved answers more than half
silently miss coherent contradictions and over
a third ignore coherent updates. The failures
persist across generator and judge families, the
behavioral detectors agree with blind human an-
notators as closely as the annotators agree with
each other, and row-level intervention traces
localize failures to retrieval, reranking, or gen-
eration. Artifact (protocol, prompts, detectors,

evidence retrieved, was the answer correct, and
was the answer supported by the retrieved context?
These are important questions, but they miss a dif-
ferent one: would the answer have changed if the
retrieved evidence had changed?

answer only when retrieved evidence is sufficient,
(2) abstain when it is removed, (3) follow re-
trieved updates, (4) acknowledge unresolved con-

tractors. The corresponding behavioral failures

surement complication that can mask dependence

Conclusion
For RAG systems that promise to answer from
retrieved evidence, observational diagnostics ask
the wrong question. Whether an answer is con-
sistent with the realized context tells us nothing
about whether the system would still produce that
answer if the evidence were removed, updated, or
contradicted. COUNTERMEM operationalizes the
counterfactual: it intervenes on the retrieved state,
regenerates with the same generator and prompt,
and measures the behavioral transition.
The protocol exposes failures invisible to aggre-
gate scoring. On RAGBench’s 27-configuration
sweep, same-dataset matched-faithfulness pairs dif-
fer by up to 0.31 in update following and 0.29
in conflict acknowledgment (n=31 matched-faith
pairs).
On six datasets, 38.8% [34.4, 43.4] of
RAGChecker-approved answers silently ignore a
coherent retrieved update and 55.6% [51.0, 60.1]
miss a coherent contradiction (Wilson 95% CIs
over the judged-valid subset, n=446). The same
intervention trace localizes the pipeline stage to
repair: matched repairs produce large gains on
retrieval- and rerank-broken fixtures (+0.40 and
+0.54 reactive rate), a significant gain on the nat-
ural HotpotQA generator class (+0.37 vs. naive
pool/k expansion), and a smaller non-significant
gain on the engineered generator fixture. The fail-
ure rates persist when the generator is replaced by
GPT-5.4-mini or Qwen3-8B and when the judge
is replaced by an out-of-family model, and the de-
tectors behind them agree with blind human labels
as closely as two annotators agree with each other.
This lets practitioners select, debug, and audit RAG
configurations against requirements that aggregate
evaluators cannot enforce alone.
Limitations
The protocol depends on the chosen interventions
and detectors.
Update and contradiction pay-
loads are LLM-synthesized rather than human-
curated. A per-row Claude-Sonnet audit of all
593 coherence-conditioned contradictions finds
93.6% well-formed; a separate stratified audit of
the broader 27-configuration sweep (n=50 per
class; Appendix J) finds Delete-All, update, and
contradiction payloads 100%, 96%, and 82% well-
formed—the lower contradiction figure reflects the
sweep’s one-line templated payloads, not the co-
herent passages behind the headline rates, which
are computed on the judged-valid subset. Holding
the payloads fixed across generators (§5.4) isolates
dependence on the generator under test but does
not test the payload synthesizer: every payload is
written by Claude-Haiku. The behavioral detec-
tors are validated against blind human labels on
n=100 items (Appendix H); the update-following
taxonomy is subjective at the adopted/mixed bound-
ary. Answer-similarity detectors can miss small
but consequential factual edits, and cluster-deletion
granularity defines the unit of evidence removal.
Sample sizes vary by cell: pooled headline rates
are computed over 446 RAGChecker-approved an-
swers with valid contradictions, but per-dataset
cells (especially TechQA, n=31) carry wider inter-
vals (roughly ±16 points for TechQA). COUNTER-
MEM is behavioral and pipeline-level: it observes
whether outputs change under counterfactual re-
trieved states and at which stage an intervention
was lost, not which internal computation produced
the answer. Finally, COUNTERMEM reports a pro-

I
Update vs. Contradiction Framing
The two counterfactual-addition probes share the
generator prompt (“Answer ONLY using the pro-
vided context. If context is insufficient or contradic-
tory, say you don’t know.”) and differ only in the
appended passage. Both passages are synthesized
by Claude-Haiku from the question and the refer-
ence answer and assert a specific alternative an-
swer of the same factual type. The update passage
is written to supersede: it presents the alternative
as the new correct answer (“Recent sources have
established that ...”). The contradiction passage
is written to compete: it asserts the alternative as
fact, with no temporal cue, so that the context now
carries two incompatible claims of equal standing.
The expected behavior therefore differs: under an
update, an evidence-bound system should adopt
the new value (adopted; failure is ignored, with
mixed and abstain as intermediate labels); under a
contradiction, it should surface the disagreement
(conflict_ack; failure is silent_pick of the injected
value or confident_match to the original, with ab-
stain as the cautious label). The judge receives the
question, the reference answer, the injected value,
and the system answer, and returns exactly one of
the four labels.
